notes.front: What are gross receipts on Schedule C?
notes.back: The total a business takes in from its trade or business, entered on line 1 of Schedule C before any costs.
notes.explanation: Amounts shown on Forms 1099-NEC belong in this line, and a shortfall against them must be explained.
notes.example: Like a till’s total takings for the year, before paying for stock, rent or wages.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule C (Form 1040) (2025), “Line 1”, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: Enter gross receipts from your trade or business. Be sure to check any Forms 1099 you received for business income that must be reported on this line.

notes.front: What is cost of goods sold (COGS)?
notes.back: The cost of the goods a business sold in the year, deducted from gross receipts and worked out from opening and closing inventory.
notes.explanation: It applies to any business that makes, buys or sells goods, not to a pure personal service business.
notes.example: Like a shop’s cost of the stock that actually left the shelves this year, not the stock still in the back room.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “How To Figure Cost of Goods Sold”, PDF p. 28
notes.evidence: If you make or buy goods to sell, you can deduct the cost of goods sold from your gross receipts on Schedule C (Form 1040). However, to determine these costs, you must value your inventory at the beginning and end of each tax year.

notes.front: Who is a small business taxpayer?
notes.back: A taxpayer with average annual gross receipts of $31 million or less for the 3 prior tax years that is not a tax shelter.
notes.explanation: The status unlocks simpler rules, such as the choice not to keep an inventory.
notes.example: Like a size band on a ticket: under the line, the simpler rules apply.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “Inventories: Small business taxpayer”, PDF p. 16
notes.evidence: You qualify as a small business taxpayer if you (a) have average annual gross receipts of $31 million or less for the 3 prior tax years (indexed for inflation), and (b) are not a tax shelter

notes.front: What are the uniform capitalization rules (UNICAP)?
notes.back: Rules requiring direct costs and part of indirect costs of producing or reselling property to be added to its basis, not deducted currently.
notes.explanation: The capitalised costs come back later through depreciation, amortisation or cost of goods sold.
notes.example: Like adding a share of the warehouse rent to the cost of each crate stored there, instead of expensing the rent at once.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “Uniform Capitalization Rules”, PDF p. 17
notes.evidence: Under the uniform capitalization rules, you must capitalize the direct costs and part of the indirect costs for production or resale activities. Include these costs in the basis of property you produce or acquire for resale, rather than claiming them as a current deduction.

notes.front: What are the at-risk rules?
notes.back: Rules limiting losses from most activities to the amount the taxpayer has at risk in the activity.
notes.explanation: A loss they disallow is treated as a deduction from the same activity in the next tax year.
notes.example: Like a stake at a card table: you can lose only what you could actually be made to pay.
notes.source: Publication 925 (2025), Passive Activity and At-Risk Rules, “At-Risk Limits”, PDF p. 19
notes.evidence: The at-risk rules limit your losses from most activities to your amount at risk in the activity. You treat any loss that is disallowed because of the at-risk limits as a deduction from the same activity in the next tax year.

notes.front: What is an excess business loss?
notes.back: The disallowed part of a business loss, figured on Form 461, added back to income and carried forward as a net operating loss.
notes.explanation: The limit was made permanent, and its threshold is indexed for inflation after 2025.
notes.example: Like a cap on how much of a bad trading year can be set against wages this year; the rest waits for later years.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “Excess business loss limitation”, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: Use Form 461 to determine the amount of your excess business loss, if any. Your excess business loss will be included as income on line 8p of Schedule 1 (Form 1040) and treated as a net operating loss (NOL) that you must carry forward

notes.front: What is an ordinary and necessary expense?
notes.back: A business expense that is common and accepted in the field (ordinary) and helpful and appropriate for the business (necessary).
notes.explanation: To be deductible, a business expense must meet both tests.
notes.example: Like a plumber’s van insurance: every plumber has it, and it helps the business run.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “Business Expenses”, PDF p. 32
notes.evidence: To be deductible, a business expense must be both ordinary and necessary. An ordinary expense is one that is common and accepted in your field of business. A necessary expense is one that is helpful and appropriate for your business.

notes.front: What is a fringe benefit?
notes.back: A form of pay for the performance of services, such as letting an employee commute in a business vehicle.
notes.explanation: Unless the law specifically excludes it, its value is taxable pay.
notes.example: Like a gym membership the employer pays for: part of the pay package, but not cash.
notes.source: Publication 15-B (2025), Employer’s Tax Guide to Fringe Benefits, “Fringe Benefit Overview”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: A fringe benefit is a form of pay for the performance of services. For example, you provide an employee with a fringe benefit when you allow the employee to use a business vehicle to commute to and from work.

notes.front: What is a statutory employee?
notes.back: A worker who is an independent contractor under common-law rules but is treated as an employee by statute for certain employment tax purposes.
notes.explanation: Only four categories of worker can qualify, and each must also meet three conditions.
notes.example: Like a commission sales rep who runs their own diary but still has social security tax withheld.
notes.source: Publication 15-A (2025), Employer’s Supplemental Tax Guide, “Statutory Employees”, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: If workers are independent contractors under the common-law rules, such workers may nevertheless be treated as employees by statute (also known as statutory employees) for certain employment tax purposes.

notes.front: What is a self-rental?
notes.back: Renting property to a trade or business activity in which the owner materially participates; the net rental income is treated as nonpassive.
notes.explanation: The rule does not apply to rent under a written binding contract entered into before 19 February 1988.
notes.example: Like a dentist who owns the surgery building and rents it to her own practice.
notes.source: Publication 925 (2025), Passive Activity and At-Risk Rules, “Rental of Property to a Nonpassive Activity”, PDF p. 17
notes.evidence: If you rent property to a trade or business activity in which you materially participated, net rental income from the property is treated as nonpassive income.

notes.front: What are business start-up costs?
notes.back: Expenses incurred before a business actually begins operating, such as advertising, travel, surveys and training.
notes.explanation: They are generally capital expenses, though a limited amount can be deducted by election.
notes.example: Like the market research and staff training a café pays for before it opens its doors.
notes.source: Publication 583 (Rev. December 2024), Starting a Business and Keeping Records, “Business Start-Up Costs”, PDF p. 9
notes.evidence: Business start-up costs are the expenses you incur before you actually begin business operations. Your business start-up costs will depend on the type of business you are starting. They may include costs for advertising, travel, surveys, and training. These costs are generally capital expenses.

notes.front: What are organizational costs?
notes.back: Costs of setting up a corporation (section 248) or a partnership (section 709) as an entity.
notes.explanation: Like start-up costs, a limited amount can be deducted and the rest amortised.
notes.example: Like the legal fees for drafting a new company’s charter, as opposed to its pre-opening advertising.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 4562 (2025), “Startup and organizational costs”, PDF p. 18
notes.evidence: You can elect to amortize the following costs for setting up your business. • Business startup costs (section 195). • Organizational costs for a corporation (section 248). • Organizational costs for a partnership (section 709).

notes.front: What is depletion?
notes.back: The using up of natural resources by mining, quarrying, drilling or cutting, deducted by the owner or operator.
notes.explanation: The deduction lets the owner account for the reduction of a product’s reserves.
notes.example: Like depreciation, but for a gravel pit that shrinks as the gravel is sold.
notes.source: Publication 225 (2025), Farmer’s Tax Guide, “Depletion”, PDF p. 49
notes.evidence: Depletion is the using up of natural resources by mining, quarrying, drilling, or cutting. The depletion deduction allows an owner or operator to account for the reduction of a product’s reserves.

notes.front: What is a business bad debt?
notes.back: A loss from a worthless debt created or acquired in the business, or closely related to it when it became worthless.
notes.explanation: A debt is closely related when the primary motive for it was a business reason.
notes.example: Like an unpaid invoice from a customer who went bust.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “Bad Debts”, PDF p. 32
notes.evidence: A business bad debt is a loss from the worthlessness of a debt that was either of the following. 1. Created or acquired in your business. 2. Closely related to your business when it became partly or totally worthless.

notes.front: What is a tax home?
notes.back: Generally, the regular place of business or post of duty, including its whole city or general area, wherever the family home is.
notes.explanation: Travel is deductible only when the taxpayer is away from this area.
notes.example: Like the office a consultant reports to in Denver, even though her family lives in Boulder.
notes.source: Publication 463 (2025), Travel, Gift, and Car Expenses, “Tax Home”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: Generally, your tax home is your regular place of business or post of duty, regardless of where you maintain your family home. It includes the entire city or general area in which your business or work is located.

notes.front: What is the standard mileage rate?
notes.back: A set amount per business mile for the cost of operating a car, used instead of deducting actual car expenses.
notes.explanation: In a year the rate is used, actual costs such as fuel, repairs and depreciation can’t also be deducted.
notes.example: Like a flat fee per mile on a taxi meter, instead of adding up every fuel receipt.
notes.source: Publication 463 (2025), Travel, Gift, and Car Expenses, “Standard Mileage Rate”, PDF p. 20
notes.evidence: If you use the standard mileage rate for a year, you can’t deduct your actual car expenses for that year.

notes.front: What is an involuntary conversion?
notes.back: Property destroyed, stolen, condemned or disposed of under threat of condemnation, with money or other property received in payment.
notes.explanation: Payment may come as insurance proceeds or a condemnation award; conversions are also called involuntary exchanges.
notes.example: Like a warehouse burned down and replaced with the insurer’s cheque.
notes.source: Publication 544 (2025), Sales and Other Dispositions of Assets, “Involuntary Conversions”, PDF p. 9
notes.evidence: An involuntary conversion occurs when your property is destroyed, stolen, condemned, or disposed of under the threat of condemnation and you receive other property or money in payment, such as insurance or a condemnation award.

notes.front: What is a specified service trade or business (SSTB)?
notes.back: A trade or business providing services in listed fields, such as health, law and accounting, whose QBI is limited at higher incomes.
notes.explanation: Above the phase-in range an SSTB’s income stops qualifying for the QBI deduction.
notes.example: Like a medical or law practice, where the owners’ skill is the product.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8995-A (2025), “Specified Service Trades or Businesses”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: An SSTB is any trade or business providing services in the fields of: • Health, including physicians, pharmacists, nurses, dentists, veterinarians, physical therapists, psychologists, and other similar healthcare professionals.

notes.front: What is unadjusted basis immediately after acquisition (UBIA)?
notes.back: For qualified property in the QBI calculation, its basis on the date it was placed in service.
notes.explanation: It feeds the alternative wage-and-property limit on the QBI deduction.
notes.example: Like the price tag on a machine the day it started work, ignoring later depreciation.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8995-A (2025), “Determining your UBIA of qualified property”, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: For purposes of determining your UBIA for all qualified property, the unadjusted basis immediately after acquisition means the basis on the placed-in-service date.

notes.front: What is the general business credit?
notes.back: The combined group of business credits, each figured on its own source form and claimed together on Form 3800.
notes.explanation: Unused amounts can generally be carried back and forward.
notes.example: Like a basket holding separate vouchers, such as the research and disabled access credits, cashed at one till.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 3800 (2025), “Who Must File”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: You must file Form 3800 and the credit source form(s) to claim any of the general business credits.

notes.front: What must a Schedule C filer do if Forms 1099-NEC show more than the gross receipts reported on line 1?
notes.back: Attach a statement explaining the difference.
notes.explanation: Line 1 should include amounts properly shown on Forms 1099-NEC.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule C (Form 1040) (2025), “Line 1”, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: If the total amounts that were reported in box 1 of Forms 1099-NEC are more than the total you are reporting on line 1, attach a statement explaining the difference.

notes.front: A retailer’s till shows $106,000, of which $6,000 is state sales tax imposed on buyers that it must pay over to the state. What gross receipts does it report?
notes.choices:
A) $100,000
B) $106,000, then deduct $6,000 as a tax
C) $106,000 with no deduction
notes.choicesExplained: B includes and deducts the collected tax, which Pub. 334 says not to do. C overstates receipts.
notes.explanation: Collected sales tax is neither included in gross receipts nor deducted: $106,000 − $6,000 = $100,000.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “Taxes”, PDF p. 40
notes.evidence: Don’t deduct state and local sales taxes imposed on the buyer that you must collect and pay over to CAUTION the state or local government. Don’t include these taxes in gross receipts or sales.

notes.front: On Schedule C, cost of goods sold is the total of opening inventory, purchases, labour, materials and other costs, minus {{c1::closing inventory}}.
notes.explanation: Line 42 subtracts line 41, inventory at end of year, from the line 40 total.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “Figuring Cost of Goods Sold on Schedule C, Lines 35 Through 42”, PDF p. 29
notes.evidence: 42 Cost of goods sold. Subtract line 41 from line 40.

notes.front: A retailer’s 2025 figures: opening inventory $20,000; purchases $80,000, including $1,000 of stock taken home for family use; labour $10,000; closing inventory $25,000. What is COGS?
notes.choicesExplained: A leaves in the $1,000 taken for personal use. B leaves in the $1,000 and forgets to subtract closing inventory.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “Line 36—Purchases Less Cost of Items Withdrawn for Personal Use”, PDF p. 29
notes.evidence: If you withdraw merchandise for your personal or family use, you must exclude this cost from the total amount of merchandise you bought for sale.

notes.front: May a small business taxpayer choose not to keep an inventory?
notes.back: Yes, but its method of accounting for inventory must still clearly reflect income.
notes.explanation: Treating inventory as non-incidental materials and supplies, or following its financial accounting, meets that test.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “Inventories: Exception for small business taxpayers”, PDF p. 16
notes.evidence: If you are a small business taxpayer, you can choose not to keep an inventory, but you must still use a method of accounting for inventory that clearly reflects income.

notes.front: A distributor (not a tax shelter) had gross receipts of $28 million, $30 million and $38 million in its 3 prior tax years. Is it a small business taxpayer for 2025?
notes.back: C: no; the average is $32 million.
notes.choices:
A) Yes: two of the three years are under $31 million
B) Yes: the latest year is what counts
C) No: the average is $32 million
notes.choicesExplained: A counts years instead of averaging. B looks at one year only.
notes.explanation: ($28m + $30m + $38m) ÷ 3 = $96m ÷ 3 = $32m, which is over $31 million.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “Inventories: Small business taxpayer”, PDF p. 16
notes.evidence: have average annual gross receipts of $31 million or less for the 3 prior tax years (indexed for inflation)

notes.front: Which two kinds of activity bring a business within the uniform capitalization rules?
notes.back: Producing real or tangible personal property, and acquiring property for resale.
notes.explanation: Tangible personal property here includes a film, sound recording, videotape or book.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “Uniform Capitalization Rules”, PDF p. 17
notes.evidence: Produce real or tangible personal property. For this purpose, tangible personal property includes a film, sound recording, videotape, book, or similar property. • Acquire property for resale.

notes.front: What are the two exceptions to the uniform capitalization rules given in Pub. 334?
notes.back: Small business taxpayers, and property you produce if your indirect production costs are $200,000 or less.
notes.explanation: Either exception removes the need to capitalise indirect costs under UNICAP.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “Uniform Capitalization Rules”, PDF p. 17
notes.evidence: These rules don’t apply to the following. 1. Small business taxpayers, defined earlier under Inventories. 2. Property you produce if your indirect costs of producing the property are $200,000 or less.

notes.front: A wholesaler with average annual gross receipts of $45 million buys goods for resale and pays $300,000 to run the warehouse that stores them. What does UNICAP require for the warehouse costs?
notes.back: B: capitalise the allocable part.
notes.choices:
A) Deduct them all in 2025
B) Capitalise the allocable part into inventory cost, recovered through COGS
C) Nothing: resellers are exempt
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores UNICAP. C is wrong: acquiring property for resale is covered, and this business is too large for the small business exception.
notes.explanation: At $45 million it is not a small business taxpayer, so indirect costs of resale activity go into basis and come back as goods are sold.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “Uniform Capitalization Rules”, PDF p. 17
notes.evidence: You recover the costs through depreciation, amortization, or cost of goods sold when you use, sell, or otherwise dispose of the property.

notes.front: What amounts is a taxpayer at risk for in an activity?
notes.back: Money and adjusted basis of property contributed, and amounts borrowed for it if personally liable or secured by other property.
notes.explanation: Borrowing that the taxpayer is not personally liable for, and that is not secured by outside property, does not add to the amount at risk.
notes.source: Publication 925 (2025), Passive Activity and At-Risk Rules, “At-Risk Amounts”, PDF p. 21
notes.evidence: You’re at risk in any activity for: 1. The money and adjusted basis of property you contribute to the activity, and 2. Amounts you borrow for use in the activity if: a. You’re personally liable for repayment, or

notes.front: Who is subject to the at-risk limits?
notes.back: Individuals (including partners and S corporation shareholders), estates, trusts and certain closely held C corporations.
notes.explanation: For this rule a C corporation is closely held if five or fewer individuals own more than 50% of its stock in the last half of the year.
notes.source: Publication 925 (2025), Passive Activity and At-Risk Rules, “Who Is Affected?”, PDF p. 19
notes.evidence: The at-risk limits apply to individuals (including partners and S corporation shareholders), estates, trusts, and certain closely held C corporations.

notes.front: Maya puts $10,000 cash into a new business activity. The activity also borrows $30,000 on a loan for which she is not personally liable and which is secured only by the activity’s own equipment. Her 2025 loss from it is $25,000. How much can the at-risk rules allow?
notes.choicesExplained: B counts the loan she is not liable for. C ignores her cash contribution.
notes.explanation: At risk = $10,000 cash; the loan meets neither borrowing test. $25,000 − $10,000 = $15,000 treated as a deduction of the activity next year.
notes.source: Publication 925 (2025), Passive Activity and At-Risk Rules, “At-Risk Amounts”, PDF p. 21
notes.evidence: You’re at risk in any activity for: 1. The money and adjusted basis of property you contribute to the activity

notes.front: Where does a sole proprietor report a canceled business debt that must be included in income?
notes.back: On line 6 of Schedule C.
notes.explanation: A canceled nonbusiness debt goes on Schedule 1 (Form 1040) instead.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “Canceled Debt: General Rule”, PDF p. 23
notes.evidence: Report the canceled amount on line 6 of Schedule C (Form 1040) if you incurred the debt in your business.

notes.front: A cash-method sole proprietor owes a supplier $2,000 for cleaning services to her shop. She has not paid it, and the supplier forgives the whole bill. Does she have income?
notes.back: B: no income.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, $2,000 on Schedule C
B) No: paying it would have been deductible
C) Yes, $1,000
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the deductible-debt exception. C invents a partial rule.
notes.explanation: Had she paid the $2,000 it would have been a deductible business expense, so its cancellation is not income.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “Canceled Debt: Exceptions”, PDF p. 23
notes.evidence: You do not realize income from a canceled debt to the extent the payment of the debt would have led to a deduction.

notes.front: A business owner’s liabilities exceed his assets by $15,000 just before a lender cancels $20,000 of business debt. The cancellation is outside bankruptcy. How much is income?
notes.choicesExplained: B excludes more than the insolvency. C ignores the insolvency exclusion.
notes.explanation: Exclusion is limited to the extent of insolvency: $20,000 − $15,000 = $5,000 included.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “Canceled Debt: Exclusions”, PDF p. 24
notes.evidence: The cancellation takes place when you are insolvent. You can exclude the canceled debt to the extent you are insolvent.

notes.front: A freelance designer pays $1,200 for a mobile phone plan and uses the phone 70% for business. What may she deduct on Schedule C?
notes.choicesExplained: B deducts the personal part. C deducts only the personal share.
notes.explanation: The personal part is separated out: $1,200 × 70% = $840 business.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “Business Expenses”, PDF p. 32
notes.evidence: The personal part is generally not deductible.

notes.front: Which expense of a small bakery is least likely to be ordinary and necessary?
notes.back: A: the family holiday.
notes.choices:
A) The owner’s family holiday flights
B) Food safety course for its staff
C) Flour and sugar
notes.choicesExplained: C and B are common in the trade and help the business run.
notes.explanation: A personal holiday is neither common in baking nor appropriate to the business.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “Business Expenses”, PDF p. 32
notes.evidence: An ordinary expense is one that is common and accepted in your field of business. A necessary expense is one that is helpful and appropriate for your business.

notes.front: Is Publication 535, Business Expenses, a current source for 2025 returns?
notes.back: No. It has been discontinued; its last revision was for 2022.
notes.explanation: Its topics are now covered in other resources, such as Pub. 334 for small businesses.
notes.source: IRS, Guide to business expense resources, “Guide to business expense resources”
notes.evidence: We have discontinued Publication 535, Business Expenses; the last revision was for 2022.

notes.front: Besides being ordinary and necessary, what two tests must employee pay meet to be deductible?
notes.back: It must be reasonable, and it must be for services performed.
notes.explanation: The pay must also be paid or incurred in the tax year.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “Employees’ Pay”, PDF p. 37
notes.evidence: In addition, the pay must meet both the following tests. For more information about fringe benefits and the exclusion of benefits, see Pub. 15-B. • The pay must be reasonable. • The pay must be for services performed.

notes.front: A sole proprietor pays herself a “salary” of $4,000 a month from the business account. What can she deduct on Schedule C for it?
notes.back: B: nothing.
notes.choices:
A) $48,000 as wages
B) Nothing
C) Half, as employer tax
notes.choicesExplained: A treats her as an employee of her own business, which she is not. C is invented.
notes.explanation: A sole proprietor is not an employee of the business, so her withdrawals are not deductible pay.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “Employees’ Pay”, PDF p. 37
notes.evidence: You can’t deduct your own salary or any personal withdrawals you make from your business. As a sole proprietor, you are not an employee of the business.

notes.front: Is a fringe benefit taxable to the recipient?
notes.back: Yes, unless the law specifically excludes it.
notes.explanation: Any benefit not excluded under the rules in section 2 of Pub. 15-B is taxable pay.
notes.source: Publication 15-B (2025), Employer’s Tax Guide to Fringe Benefits, “Are Fringe Benefits Taxable?”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: Any fringe benefit you provide is taxable and must be included in the recipient's pay unless the law specifically excludes it.

notes.front: A customer of a staffing firm provides free daycare to the firm’s employees in exchange for the firm’s services. Who is the provider of this fringe benefit?
notes.back: A: the staffing firm.
notes.choices:
A) The staffing firm
B) The customer
C) Nobody: third-party benefits are not fringe benefits
notes.choicesExplained: B looks at who hands over the benefit. C is wrong: the benefit is still pay for services.
notes.explanation: The benefit is provided for services performed for the firm, so the firm is treated as its provider.
notes.source: Publication 15-B (2025), Employer’s Tax Guide to Fringe Benefits, “Provider of benefit”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: You’re considered the provider of a fringe benefit even if a third party, such as your client or customer, provides the benefit to your employee for services the employee performs for you.

notes.front: At the holidays an employer gives each employee a $25 supermarket gift card. Is it an excludable de minimis benefit?
notes.back: C: no; it is taxable pay.
notes.choices:
A) Yes: $25 is a small amount
B) Yes, if given only once a year
C) No: cash equivalents are never de minimis
notes.choicesExplained: A and B look at size and frequency, but gift cards are excluded from de minimis treatment however small.
notes.explanation: Gift cards and gift certificates are cash equivalents.
notes.source: Publication 15-B (2025), Employer’s Tax Guide to Fringe Benefits, “De Minimis (Minimal) Benefits”, PDF p. 9
notes.evidence: Cash and cash equivalent fringe benefits (for example, gift certificates, gift cards, and the use of a charge card or credit card), no matter how little, are never excludable as a de minimis benefit.

notes.front: When are wages for a child under 18 who works for a parent exempt from social security and Medicare taxes?
notes.back: When the business is a sole proprietorship, or a partnership in which each partner is a parent of the child.
notes.explanation: The work must be in the parent’s trade or business for this under-18 rule.
notes.source: Publication 15 (2025), (Circular E), Employer’s Tax Guide, “Family Employees: Child employed by parents”, PDF p. 15
notes.evidence: Payments for the services of a child under age 18 who works for their parent in a trade or business aren't subject to social security and Medicare taxes if the trade or business is a sole proprietorship or a partnership in which each partner is a parent of the child.

notes.front: A 16-year-old works in her mother’s business, which is a corporation wholly owned by the mother. Are her wages subject to social security and Medicare taxes?
notes.back: C: yes.
notes.choices:
A) No: she is under 18 and works for a parent
B) No, if the corporation is an S corporation
C) Yes: work for a corporation is covered even if a parent controls it
notes.choicesExplained: A applies the sole proprietorship rule to a corporation. B: the rule makes no exception for S corporations.
notes.explanation: The family exemption does not reach wages paid by a corporation.
notes.source: Publication 15 (2025), (Circular E), Employer’s Tax Guide, “Covered services of a child or spouse”, PDF p. 15
notes.evidence: The wages for the services of a child or spouse are subject to income tax withholding as well as social security, Medicare, and FUTA taxes if they work for: • A corporation, even if it is controlled by the child's parent

notes.front: Which employment taxes apply to wages one spouse pays the other in a trade or business?
notes.back: Income tax withholding, social security and Medicare taxes, but not federal unemployment tax.
notes.explanation: Domestic work for a spouse outside a trade or business, such as in a private home, is free of social security, Medicare and federal unemployment taxes.
notes.source: Publication 15 (2025), (Circular E), Employer’s Tax Guide, “One spouse employed by another”, PDF p. 15
notes.evidence: The wages for the services of an individual who works for their spouse in a trade or business are subject to income tax withholding and social security and Medicare taxes, but not to FUTA tax.

notes.front: Does an employer withhold federal income tax from a statutory employee’s wages?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: The employer still gives a Form W-2 with the "Statutory employee" box checked.
notes.source: Publication 15-A (2025), Employer’s Supplemental Tax Guide, “Statutory Employees: Income tax”, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: Don't withhold federal income tax from the wages of statutory employees.

notes.front: Where does a statutory employee report box 1 income from a Form W-2 with the statutory employee box checked?
notes.back: On line 1 of Schedule C, with related expenses on Schedule C.
notes.explanation: Social security and Medicare tax was already withheld, so no self-employment tax is owed on it.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule C (Form 1040) (2025), “Statutory employees”, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: Enter your statutory employee income from box 1 of Form W-2 on line 1 of Schedule C and check the box on that line. Social security and Medicare tax should have been withheld from your earnings; as a result, you do not owe self-employment tax on these earnings.

notes.front: Which worker can fall in a statutory employee category?
notes.back: A: the life insurance agent.
notes.choices:
A) A full-time life insurance agent selling mainly for one company
B) A freelance web designer with many clients
C) A plumber who owns his van and tools
notes.choicesExplained: B and C fit none of the four categories: drivers, life insurance agents, home workers and traveling salespersons.
notes.explanation: A full-time life insurance sales agent whose principal business is selling for one company is category 2.
notes.source: Publication 15-A (2025), Employer’s Supplemental Tax Guide, “Statutory Employees”, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: A full-time life insurance sales agent whose principal business activity is selling life insurance or annuity contracts, or both, primarily for one life insurance company.

notes.front: When is rent paid to a related person reasonable?
notes.back: When it is the same amount the business would pay a stranger for the same property.
notes.explanation: Reasonableness ordinarily becomes an issue only between related parties; rent based on a percentage of gross receipts is not unreasonable for that reason alone.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “Rent Expense: Unreasonable rent”, PDF p. 39
notes.evidence: Rent paid to a related person is reasonable if it is the same amount you would pay to a stranger for use of the same property.

notes.front: On 1 July 2025 a calendar-year shop pays $24,000 for 24 months’ rent in advance. How much can it deduct for 2025?
notes.choicesExplained: A deducts it all when paid. B uses a full year though only 6 months fall in 2025.
notes.explanation: $24,000 ÷ 24 = $1,000 a month; July–December = 6 months × $1,000 = $6,000.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “Rent Expense: Rent paid in advance”, PDF p. 39
notes.evidence: If you pay rent in advance, you can deduct only the amount that applies to your use of the rented property during the tax

notes.front: Leo owns a building and rents it to his S corporation, in whose business he materially participates. The rent nets him $18,000. He also has a $10,000 loss from an unrelated passive partnership. How is the $18,000 treated?
notes.back: A: nonpassive.
notes.choices:
A) Nonpassive, so it cannot absorb the passive loss
B) Passive, so it absorbs the $10,000 loss
C) Exempt income
notes.choicesExplained: B treats it as ordinary rental income, ignoring the recharacterisation. C is invented.
notes.explanation: Net rental income from property rented to an activity in which he materially participates is nonpassive.
notes.source: Publication 925 (2025), Passive Activity and At-Risk Rules, “Rental of Property to a Nonpassive Activity”, PDF p. 17
notes.evidence: If you rent property to a trade or business activity in which you materially participated, net rental income from the property is treated as nonpassive income.

notes.front: How much of its business start-up costs can a taxpayer elect to deduct in the first year?
notes.back: Up to $5,000, reduced by the amount by which start-up costs exceed $50,000.
notes.explanation: Start-up costs left over are amortised over 180 months, starting with the month the business began.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule C (Form 1040) (2025), “Line 27a: Business startup costs”, PDF p. 16
notes.evidence: can elect to deduct up to $5,000 of certain business startup costs. The $5,000 limit is reduced (but not below zero) by the amount by which your total startup costs exceed $50,000.

notes.front: Start-up and organizational costs not deducted in the first year are amortised ratably over {{c1::180}} months.
notes.explanation: The amortisation period starts with the month business operations begin.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 4562 (2025), “Startup and organizational costs”, PDF p. 18
notes.evidence: Any cost not deducted currently must be amortized ratably over a 180-month period. The amortization period starts with the month you begin business operations.

notes.front: A new business incurs $53,000 of start-up costs and opens on 1 January 2025. How much can it deduct in 2025 in total (first-year deduction plus 12 months’ amortisation)?
notes.choicesExplained: B forgets the phase-down and the amortisation. C forgets the amortisation.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule C (Form 1040) (2025), “Line 27a: Business startup costs”, PDF p. 16
notes.evidence: The $5,000 limit is reduced (but not below zero) by the amount by which your total startup costs exceed $50,000. Your remaining startup costs can be amortized over a 180-month period beginning with the month the business began.

notes.front: A corporation filed its return on time but forgot to elect to deduct start-up costs. Can it still elect?
notes.back: Yes, on an amended return filed within 6 months of the return’s due date (excluding extensions).
notes.explanation: The amended return must be marked “Filed pursuant to section 301.9100-2”.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120 (2025), “Election to deduct business start-up and organizational costs”, PDF p. 11
notes.evidence: If the corporation timely filed its return for the year without making an election, it can still make an election by filing an amended return within 6 months of the due date of the return (excluding extensions).

notes.front: Which depletion method must be used for standing timber, and which for mineral property?
notes.back: Timber: cost depletion. Mineral property: generally whichever of cost or percentage depletion gives the larger deduction.
notes.explanation: These are the only two ways of figuring depletion.
notes.source: Publication 225 (2025), Farmer’s Tax Guide, “Figuring Depletion”, PDF p. 49
notes.evidence: Percentage depletion. For mineral property, you must generally use the method that gives you the larger deduction. For standing timber, you must use cost depletion.

notes.front: When can a business deduct an uncollectible account receivable as a bad debt?
notes.back: Only if the amount was included in gross income for the year of the deduction or an earlier year.
notes.explanation: Accrual-method businesses usually meet this because they report income as earned.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “Bad Debts”, PDF p. 32
notes.evidence: You can take a bad debt deduction for these accounts and notes receivable only if the amount CAUTION you were owed was included in your gross income either for the year the deduction is claimed or for a prior year.

notes.front: A cash-method consultant billed a client $8,000 in 2025. The client went bankrupt and will never pay. What bad debt deduction can the consultant take?
notes.choices:
A) $8,000 business bad debt
B) $0
C) $8,000 nonbusiness bad debt
notes.choicesExplained: A and C deduct income that was never reported.
notes.explanation: Under the cash method the $8,000 was never included in income, so there is nothing to write off.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “Bad Debts: Cash method”, PDF p. 32
notes.evidence: You can’t take a bad debt deduction for amounts owed to you that you have not received and can’t collect if you never included those amounts in income.

notes.front: When is a taxpayer traveling away from home for tax purposes?
notes.back: When duties keep them away from their tax home’s general area substantially longer than a day’s work, and they need sleep or rest.
notes.explanation: Napping in the car does not meet the rest requirement.
notes.source: Publication 463 (2025), Travel, Gift, and Car Expenses, “Traveling Away From Home”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: Your duties require you to be away from the general area of your tax home (defined later) substantially longer than an ordinary day’s work, and • You need to sleep or rest to meet the demands of your

notes.front: An engineer based in Atlanta takes a job in Seattle that is realistically expected to last 18 months. Can he deduct his Seattle living costs as travel?
notes.back: B: no.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, for the first 12 months
B) No: the assignment is indefinite and Seattle becomes his tax home
C) Yes, for the whole 18 months
notes.choicesExplained: A and C treat it as temporary; an assignment expected to exceed 1 year is indefinite from the start.
notes.explanation: An indefinite job location becomes the new tax home, so he is not away from home there.
notes.source: Publication 463 (2025), Travel, Gift, and Car Expenses, “Temporary Assignment or Job”, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: An assignment or job in a single location is considered indefinite if it is realistically expected to last for more than 1 year, whether or not it actually lasts for more than 1 year.

notes.front: What share of the cost of business meals can generally be deducted?
notes.explanation: The owner or an employee must be present, and the meal must not be lavish or extravagant.
notes.source: Publication 463 (2025), Travel, Gift, and Car Expenses, “50% limit on meals”, PDF p. 7
notes.evidence: regardless of the method you use, you can generally deduct only 50% of the unreimbursed cost of your meals.

notes.front: Can a business deduct expenses for entertainment, amusement or recreation?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: Business meals, by contrast, remain 50% deductible.
notes.source: Publication 463 (2025), Travel, Gift, and Car Expenses, “2. Meals and Entertainment”, PDF p. 13
notes.evidence: You can no longer take a deduction for any expense related to activities generally considered entertainment, amusement, or recreation.

notes.front: A consultant spends $400 on dinners with clients (she attends, nothing lavish) and $600 on basketball tickets for the same clients. What may she deduct?
notes.choicesExplained: B applies 50% to the tickets too. C ignores both rules.
notes.explanation: Meals: $400 × 50% = $200. Tickets are entertainment: $0. Total $200.
notes.source: Publication 463 (2025), Travel, Gift, and Car Expenses, “2. Meals and Entertainment”, PDF p. 13
notes.evidence: You can continue to deduct 50% of the cost of business meals if you (or your employee) are present and the food or beverages aren’t considered lavish or extravagant.

notes.front: What is the most a business can deduct for gifts to one person in a tax year?
notes.explanation: Gifts to a company meant for a particular person count as indirect gifts to that person.
notes.source: Publication 463 (2025), Travel, Gift, and Car Expenses, “Gifts: $25 limit”, PDF p. 16
notes.evidence: You can deduct no more than $25 for business gifts you give directly or indirectly to each person during your tax year.

notes.front: A sole proprietor gives each of 5 clients a $40 bottle of wine, plus $2 of gift wrap each. What can he deduct?
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the $25 limit. B forgets the incidental wrapping.
notes.explanation: Wrapping is incidental and outside the limit. Wine: $25 × 5 = $125; wrapping: $2 × 5 = $10; $125 + $10 = $135.
notes.source: Publication 463 (2025), Travel, Gift, and Car Expenses, “Gifts: Incidental costs”, PDF p. 17
notes.evidence: Incidental costs, such as engraving on jewelry, or packaging, insuring, and mailing, are generally not included in determining the cost of a gift for purposes of the $25 limit.

notes.front: If both spouses give business gifts to the same person, how is the $25 limit applied?
notes.back: The spouses are treated as one taxpayer, so one $25 limit applies.
notes.explanation: Separate businesses or separate connections to the recipient do not change this.
notes.source: Publication 463 (2025), Travel, Gift, and Car Expenses, “Gifts”, PDF p. 17
notes.evidence: If you and your spouse both give gifts, both of you are treated as one taxpayer. It doesn’t matter whether you have separate businesses, are separately employed, or whether each of you has an independent connection with the recipient.

notes.front: What is the standard mileage rate for business use of a car in 2025?
notes.back: 70 cents a mile.
notes.explanation: Pub. 334 already shows 72.5 cents for 2026; do not mix the years.
notes.source: Publication 463 (2025), Travel, Gift, and Car Expenses, “Standard Mileage Rate”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: For 2025, the standard mileage rate for the cost of operating your car for business use is 70 cents ($0.70) per mile.

notes.front: In 2025 a sole proprietor drives 12,000 business miles in her own car, using the standard mileage rate, and pays $300 in business parking and tolls. What is her car deduction?
notes.choicesExplained: A leaves out parking and tolls, which are deductible in addition. C uses a wrong rate.
notes.explanation: Tolls and parking sit outside the per-mile rate: 12,000 × $0.70 = $8,400; + $300 = $8,700.
notes.source: Publication 463 (2025), Travel, Gift, and Car Expenses, “Parking fees and tolls”, PDF p. 21
notes.evidence: In addition to using the standard mileage rate, you can deduct any business-related parking fees and tolls.

notes.front: When must the standard mileage rate be chosen for a car you own?
notes.back: In the first year the car is available for use in your business.
notes.explanation: In later years the owner may choose either the rate or actual expenses.
notes.source: Publication 463 (2025), Travel, Gift, and Car Expenses, “Choosing the standard mileage rate”, PDF p. 20
notes.evidence: If you want to use the standard mileage rate for a car you own, you must choose to use it in the first year the car is available for use in your business.

notes.front: A contractor using actual expenses drives 25,000 miles in 2025, 15,000 of them for business. His car costs (fuel, insurance, repairs, depreciation) total $10,000. What is his business deduction?
notes.choicesExplained: A deducts personal use. C applies the personal share.
notes.source: Publication 463 (2025), Travel, Gift, and Car Expenses, “Actual Car Expenses: Business and personal use”, PDF p. 21
notes.evidence: If you use your car for both business and personal purposes, you must divide your expenses between business and personal use. You can divide your expense based on the miles driven for each purpose.

notes.front: How do the standard mileage rate and the actual expenses method differ for a car?
notes.back: The rate multiplies business miles by a set amount; actual expenses apportions real costs, including depreciation, by business use.
notes.explanation: In a year the rate is used, the actual costs it replaces cannot also be deducted.
notes.source: Publication 463 (2025), Travel, Gift, and Car Expenses, “Actual Car Expenses”, PDF p. 21
notes.evidence: If you don’t use the standard mileage rate, you may be able to deduct your actual car expenses. Actual car expenses include: Depreciation Licenses Gas Oil Lease payments Insurance

notes.front: What are two of the three requirements for deducting interest on a business debt?
notes.back: You are legally liable for the debt; and you and the lender intend it to be repaid.
notes.explanation: The third is a true debtor-creditor relationship; the kind of property securing the loan does not matter.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “Interest”, PDF p. 38
notes.evidence: You can deduct interest on a debt only if you meet all of the following requirements. • You are legally liable for that debt. • Both you and the lender intend that the debt be repaid. • You and the lender have a true debtor-creditor relationship.

notes.front: A self-employed florist pays $900 of 2025 interest on her van loan and uses the van 75% for business. How much goes on Schedule C?
notes.choicesExplained: B includes the personal share. C puts only the personal share on Schedule C.
notes.explanation: $900 × 75% = $675 business interest. The personal part cannot go on Schedule C.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “Interest: Interest on car loans”, PDF p. 38
notes.evidence: If you are self-employed and use your vehicle in your business, you can deduct the part of the interest expense that represents your business use of the vehicle on Schedule C (Form 1040).

notes.front: For 2025, what must be added back to taxable income when figuring adjusted taxable income for the business interest limit?
notes.back: The deductions for depreciation, amortisation and depletion.
notes.explanation: Form 8990 figures whether business interest expense is limited.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “Interest”, PDF p. 38
notes.evidence: For tax years beginning in 2025, the calculation of adjusted taxable income includes a requirement to add back to taxable income the deductions for depreciation, amortization, and depletion

notes.front: A calendar-year business pays $3,600 on 1 October 2025 for a three-year liability policy starting that day. How much can it deduct for 2025?
notes.choicesExplained: A deducts all three years at once. C deducts a full year, though only 3 months fall in 2025.
notes.explanation: Only the part for 2025 is deductible: $3,600 ÷ 36 months = $100 a month; October to December is 3 × $100 = $300.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “Expenses paid in advance”, PDF p. 15
notes.evidence: You can deduct an expense you pay in advance only in the year to which it applies.

notes.front: Can a sole proprietor deduct federal income tax, or a state tax on net income, on Schedule C?
notes.back: No. Federal income tax is not deductible, and state net income taxes go on Schedule A if itemising.
notes.explanation: Only a state tax on gross income directly attributable to the business goes on Schedule C.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “Taxes: Income taxes”, PDF p. 40
notes.evidence: You can deduct on Schedule C (Form 1040) a state tax on gross income (as distinguished from net income) directly attributable to your business. You can deduct other state and local income taxes on Schedule A (Form 1040) if you itemize your deductions. Do not deduct federal income tax.

notes.front: Which of these payments can a sole proprietor deduct on Schedule C?
notes.back: A: the personal property tax.
notes.choices:
A) State tax on personal property used in the business
B) A fine for breaking a city zoning law
C) Federal income tax on business profit
notes.choicesExplained: B is a penalty for breaking the law. C is federal income tax, which is never deductible.
notes.explanation: State or local tax on personal property used in the business is deductible on Schedule C.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “Taxes: Personal property tax”, PDF p. 40
notes.evidence: You can deduct on Schedule C (Form 1040) any tax imposed by a state or local government on personal property used in your business.

notes.front: Where does a sole proprietor deduct one-half of self-employment tax?
notes.back: On line 15 of Schedule 1 (Form 1040), not on Schedule C.
notes.explanation: Employer social security and Medicare taxes on employees’ wages, by contrast, are business expenses.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “Taxes: SE tax”, PDF p. 40
notes.evidence: You can deduct one-half of your SE tax on line 15 of Schedule 1 (Form 1040).

notes.front: How does a business treat sales tax it pays when buying depreciable equipment?
notes.back: As part of the equipment’s cost, added to its basis for depreciation.
notes.explanation: Sales tax on a deductible service is deducted with the service; on goods for resale it is part of their cost.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “Sales tax”, PDF p. 40
notes.evidence: Treat any sales tax you pay on a service or on the purchase or use of property as part of the cost of the service or property.

notes.front: Can an employer deduct the social security and Medicare taxes it pays from its own funds?
notes.back: Yes, along with federal unemployment tax and state unemployment fund payments.
notes.explanation: The employer’s share is a business expense, unlike the owner’s own self-employment tax.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “Taxes: Employment taxes”, PDF p. 40
notes.evidence: You can deduct the social security, Medicare, and FUTA taxes you paid out of your own funds as an employer.

notes.front: What is a casualty?
notes.back: Damage, destruction or loss of property from an identifiable event that is sudden, unexpected or unusual.
notes.explanation: A sudden event is swift rather than gradual, so slow deterioration is not a casualty.
notes.source: Publication 547 (2025), Casualties, Disasters, and Thefts, “Casualty”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: A casualty is the damage, destruction, or loss of property resulting from an identifiable event that is sudden, unexpected, or unusual. • A sudden event is one that is swift, not gradual or progressive.

notes.front: How is the loss figured when business property is stolen or completely destroyed?
notes.back: Adjusted basis, minus salvage value, minus insurance or other reimbursement received or expected.
notes.explanation: The drop in fair market value is not considered for such business property.
notes.source: Publication 547 (2025), Casualties, Disasters, and Thefts, “Business or income-producing property”, PDF p. 8
notes.evidence: If you have business or income-producing property, such as rental property, and it is stolen or completely destroyed, the decrease in FMV isn’t considered.

notes.front: A storm completely destroys a business machine with an adjusted basis of $12,000 and a fair market value of $9,000. Salvage brings $500 and insurance pays $7,000. What is the deductible loss?
notes.choicesExplained: B uses fair market value, which is ignored for destroyed business property. A forgets the salvage.
notes.explanation: Fair market value is ignored for destroyed business property: $12,000 − $500 − $7,000 = $4,500.
notes.source: Publication 547 (2025), Casualties, Disasters, and Thefts, “Business or income-producing property”, PDF p. 8
notes.evidence: Your loss is figured as follows: Your adjusted basis in the property MINUS Any salvage value MINUS Any insurance or other reimbursement you receive or expect to receive

notes.front: The state condemns a shop’s parking lot, adjusted basis $60,000, paying a net award of $95,000. What is the realised gain?
notes.choicesExplained: B ignores basis. C assumes condemnations never produce gain.
notes.explanation: Net award − adjusted basis: $95,000 − $60,000 = $35,000, which may be postponed by buying replacement property.
notes.source: Publication 544 (2025), Sales and Other Dispositions of Assets, “Gain or Loss From Condemnations”, PDF p. 10
notes.evidence: If your net condemnation award is more than the adjusted basis of the condemned property, you have a gain.

notes.front: Generally, when does the replacement period for a condemnation end?
notes.back: 2 years after the end of the first tax year in which any part of the gain is realised.
notes.explanation: Business or investment real property gets a longer period.
notes.source: Publication 544 (2025), Sales and Other Dispositions of Assets, “Replacement period”, PDF p. 15
notes.evidence: The replacement period generally ends 2 years after the end of the first tax year in which any part of the gain on the condemnation is realized.

notes.front: When condemned real property was held for business or investment, when does the replacement period end?
notes.back: 3 years after the end of the first tax year in which any part of the gain is realised.
notes.explanation: The 3 years do not apply to property held primarily for sale, or if replacement is by buying control of a corporation.
notes.source: Publication 544 (2025), Sales and Other Dispositions of Assets, “Replacement period”, PDF p. 15
notes.evidence: If real property held for use in a trade or business or for investment (not including property held primarily for sale) is condemned, the replacement period ends 3 years after the end of the first tax year in which any part of the gain on the condemnation is realized.

notes.front: A city condemns an office building a company uses in its business. The company realises gain on the award in 2025 (calendar year). By when must it buy replacement property to postpone the gain?
notes.back: C: 31 December 2028.
notes.choices:
A) 31 December 2027
B) 31 December 2026
C) 31 December 2028
notes.choicesExplained: A applies the general 2-year period. B applies 1 year.
notes.explanation: Business real property: 3 years after the end of 2025 = 31 December 2028.
notes.source: Publication 544 (2025), Sales and Other Dispositions of Assets, “Replacement period”, PDF p. 15
notes.evidence: the replacement period ends 3 years after the end of the first tax year in which any part of the gain on the condemnation is realized.

notes.front: A condemnation award of $500,000 is received for property with an adjusted basis of $300,000. Replacement property costs $450,000. How much gain must be reported?
notes.choicesExplained: A postpones nothing. B postpones gain even though not all of the award was reinvested.
notes.explanation: Gain $200,000. Unspent award: $500,000 − $450,000 = $50,000 reported; $150,000 postponed.
notes.source: Publication 544 (2025), Sales and Other Dispositions of Assets, “Postponement of Gain”, PDF p. 13
notes.evidence: If the cost of the replacement property is less than the amount realized, you must report the gain up to the unspent part of the amount realized.

notes.front: Which business is an SSTB?
notes.back: B: the accounting practice.
notes.choices:
A) A printing firm that prints legal briefs for law firms
B) An accounting practice of enrolled agents
C) A health club
notes.choicesExplained: A: services not needing skills unique to law are excluded. C: the operation of health clubs is excluded from the health field.
notes.explanation: Accounting, including enrolled agents and return preparers, is a listed field.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8995-A (2025), “Specified Service Trades or Businesses”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: Accounting, including accountants, enrolled agents, return preparers, financial auditors, and similar professionals

notes.front: Under de minimis rule 1, when is a business with $25 million or less of gross receipts not treated as an SSTB?
notes.back: When less than 10% of its gross receipts come from services in a specified service field.
notes.explanation: Above $25 million of gross receipts the threshold is 5%.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8995-A (2025), “Specified Service Trades or Businesses: De minimis rule 1”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: If your gross receipts from a trade or business are $25 million or less and less than 10% of the gross receipts are from the performance of services in a specified service field, then your trade or business isn’t considered an SSTB

notes.front: For 2025, above what taxable income (before the QBI deduction) do the SSTB and W-2 wage limits start to apply?
notes.back: $197,300; $394,600 if married filing jointly.
notes.explanation: At or below the threshold, QBI does not need to be reduced.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8995-A (2025), “General Instructions”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: if your taxable income (before the QBI deduction) exceeds the threshold ($394,600 if married filing jointly, and $197,300 for all other returns)

notes.front: A single dentist has 2025 taxable income before the QBI deduction of $180,000, all from her practice. Does the SSTB rule limit her QBI deduction?
notes.back: B: no.
notes.choices:
A) Yes: dentistry is an SSTB
B) No: her income is at or below $197,300
C) Yes, by half
notes.choicesExplained: A and C forget that the SSTB rule bites only above the threshold.
notes.explanation: $180,000 is below the $197,300 threshold, so her SSTB is treated as a qualified trade or business.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8995-A (2025), “Specified Service Trades or Businesses: Exception 1”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: If your 2025 taxable income before the QBI deduction isn’t more than $394,600 if married filing jointly, and $197,300 for all other returns, your SSTB is treated as a qualified trade or business

notes.front: For 2025, above what taxable income does an SSTB’s income no longer qualify for the QBI deduction at all?
notes.back: $247,300; $494,600 if married filing jointly.
notes.explanation: Between the threshold and these amounts, only an applicable percentage of the SSTB counts.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8995-A (2025), “Schedule A (Form 8995-A)”, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: If your taxable income is more than $247,300 ($494,600 if married filing jointly), your SSTB doesn’t qualify for the deduction.

notes.front: A married couple filing jointly has 2025 taxable income before the QBI deduction of $520,000, mostly from the husband’s law practice. How much of the law practice’s income counts as QBI?
notes.back: B: none.
notes.choices:
A) All of it
B) None
C) An applicable percentage
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the SSTB rule. C applies within the phase-in range, which ends at $494,600.
notes.explanation: $520,000 is above $494,600, so the SSTB does not qualify.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8995-A (2025), “Schedule A (Form 8995-A)”, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: If your taxable income is more than $247,300 ($494,600 if married filing jointly), your SSTB doesn’t qualify for the deduction.

notes.front: Above the threshold, to what may QBI for each trade or business be reduced?
notes.back: The greater of 50% of W-2 wages, or 25% of W-2 wages plus 2.5% of the UBIA of qualified property.
notes.explanation: The reduction phases in across the range and applies fully above it.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8995-A (2025), “General Instructions”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: your QBI for each of your trades or businesses may be partially or fully reduced to the greater of 50% of W-2 wages paid by the qualified trade or business, or 25% of W-2 wages plus 2.5% of the UBIA of qualified property

notes.front: A non-SSTB business pays W-2 wages of $100,000 and holds qualified property with UBIA of $400,000. Which amount is the wage-and-property limit?
notes.choicesExplained: A is the smaller figure; the rule takes the greater. B adds both tests together.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8995-A (2025), “General Instructions”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: the greater of 50% of W-2 wages paid by the qualified trade or business, or 25% of W-2 wages plus 2.5% of the UBIA of qualified property from the qualified trade or business.

notes.front: What ownership test must be met to aggregate trades or businesses for the W-2 wage and UBIA limits?
notes.back: The same person or group owns 50% or more of each business for most of the year, including its last day.
notes.explanation: Without aggregation, each trade or business applies the limits separately.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8995-A (2025), “Aggregation”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: You or a group of persons directly or indirectly own 50% or more of each trade or business for a majority of the tax year, including the last day of the tax year

notes.front: A company has unused general business credit from 2025 that it cannot use because of the tax liability limit. What is the first year it can generally use it, and the last?
notes.back: C: back to 2024, then forward to 2045.
notes.choices:
A) 2026 only
B) 2023, then forward to 2030
C) 2024, then forward to 2045
notes.choicesExplained: B uses a 2-year carryback and 5-year carryforward. A forgets the carryback.
notes.explanation: Carry back 1 year: 2025 − 1 = 2024. Carry forward 20 years: 2025 + 20 = 2045.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 3800 (2025), “Carryback and carryforward”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: In general, unused general business credits may be carried back 1 year and carried forward 20 years.

notes.front: Which businesses are eligible small businesses for the disabled access credit?
notes.back: Those with preceding-year gross receipts of $1 million or less, or no more than 30 full-time employees, that elect the credit.
notes.explanation: A full-time employee here works at least 30 hours a week for 20 or more weeks.
notes.source: Form 8826, Disabled Access Credit, with instructions (Rev. September 2017), “Definitions: Eligible Small Business”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: Had gross receipts (including that of any predecessor) for the preceding tax year that did not exceed $1 million or had no more than 30 full-time employees during the preceding tax year

notes.front: An eligible small business spends $8,000 to install a wheelchair ramp at its shop, built in 1975. Form 8826 uses a $250 minimum and a 50% rate. What is the credit?
notes.choicesExplained: A skips the $250 minimum. C is the maximum credit, not this one.
notes.source: Form 8826, Disabled Access Credit, with instructions (Rev. September 2017), “Form 8826, lines 1–8”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: Multiply line 5 by 50% (0.50)

notes.front: What is the most disabled access credit a taxpayer can enter on Form 8826, line 8?
notes.explanation: Line 8 adds the taxpayer’s own credit to any from partnerships and S corporations, then caps the total.
notes.source: Form 8826, Disabled Access Credit, with instructions (Rev. September 2017), “Form 8826, line 8”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: Add lines 6 and 7, but do not enter more than $5,000.

notes.front: What is a qualified small business for the research credit payroll tax election?
notes.back: A corporation or partnership with gross receipts under $5 million for the year and none before the 5-tax-year period ending that year.
notes.explanation: Such a business can apply up to $500,000 of research credit against the employer share of social security tax.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025), “Qualified Small Business (Payroll Tax Credit Election)”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: A qualified small business is a corporation (including an S corporation) or partnership with: 1. Gross receipts of less than $5 million for the tax year, and 2. No gross receipts for any tax year before the 5-tax-year period ending with the tax year.

notes.front: A software start-up, a corporation with $3 million of 2025 gross receipts and its first receipts in 2022, has a $700,000 research credit. How much can it elect to use against payroll tax?
notes.choices:
A) $700,000
B) $500,000
C) $0: payroll use needs a partnership
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the $500,000 cap. C is wrong: corporations qualify.
notes.explanation: It is a qualified small business (under $5 million; receipts only in the last 4 years), so the smaller of $700,000 and $500,000 applies.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025), “Payroll Tax Credit Election”, PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: The payroll tax credit election is an annual election made by a qualified small business specifying the amount of research credit, not to exceed $500,000, that may be used against the employer portion of social security liability.

notes.front: For the 2025 small employer health insurance credit, what average annual wage limit applies?
notes.back: Average annual wages of less than $67,000 per full-time equivalent employee.
notes.explanation: Above average wages of $33,300 (the figure the instructions’ Worksheet 6 uses) the credit shrinks, and at $67,000 or more it is reduced to zero.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8941 (2025), “Eligible Small Employer”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: You paid average annual wages for the tax year of less than $67,000 per FTE.

notes.front: For the small employer health insurance credit, what limit applies to the employer’s workforce?
notes.back: Fewer than 25 full-time equivalent employees for the tax year.
notes.explanation: An employer with exactly 25 full-time equivalents gets no credit because of the phase-out.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8941 (2025), “Eligible Small Employer”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: You had fewer than 25 full-time equivalent employees (FTEs) for the tax year.

notes.front: A taxable employer has 40 employees, each working half-time, with average annual wages of $30,000 per full-time equivalent. Does it pass the size and wage tests for Form 8941?
notes.back: B: yes.
notes.choices:
A) No: 40 employees is over 25
B) Yes: 20 full-time equivalents and wages under $67,000
C) No: part-time staff don’t count
notes.choicesExplained: A counts heads, not full-time equivalents. C is wrong: part-timers count as fractions.
notes.explanation: 40 × 0.5 = 20 full-time equivalents, fewer than 25; $30,000 is under $67,000.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8941 (2025), “Eligible Small Employer”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: You may be able to meet this requirement even if you had 25 or more employees.

notes.front: What is the maximum small employer health insurance credit for a taxable employer, and for a tax-exempt one?
notes.back: Taxable: 50% of premiums paid. Tax-exempt: 35%, claimed as a refundable credit on Form 990-T.
notes.explanation: The taxable employer’s credit is part of the general business credit.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8941 (2025), “Purpose of Form”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: For all other eligible small employers, the maximum credit is 50% of premiums paid and can be taken against both regular and alternative minimum tax. The credit is claimed as part of the general business credit on Form 3800

notes.front: Can a corporation deduct foreign income taxes in the same year it claims the foreign tax credit for them?
notes.back: No. Foreign income taxes are left out of the tax deduction if the credit is claimed.
notes.explanation: Corporations figure the credit on Form 1118.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120 (2025), “Line 17. Taxes and Licenses”, PDF p. 13
notes.evidence: Foreign or U.S. territory income taxes if a foreign tax credit is claimed.

notes.front: Which corporate net operating losses can be carried back, and for how long?
notes.back: Only farming losses and losses of a non-life insurance company, for 2 years.
notes.explanation: Other corporate NOLs are carried forward only; the carryback can also be waived.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120 (2025), “Net operating loss (NOL)”, PDF p. 17
notes.evidence: Only farming losses and losses of an insurance company (other than a life insurance company) can be carried back. The carryback period for these losses is 2 years.

notes.front: A corporation has 2025 taxable income of $100,000 before any NOL deduction (and no special deductions). It has a $150,000 NOL carryforward from 2022. What NOL deduction can it take for 2025?
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the 80% limit for post-2017 losses. B exceeds taxable income.
notes.explanation: Post-2017 NOL limited to 80% of taxable income: $100,000 × 80% = $80,000; $70,000 carries forward.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120 (2025), “Line 29a. Net Operating Loss Deduction”, PDF p. 17
notes.evidence: 80% of the excess, if any, of taxable income determined without any NOL deduction

notes.front: What does the exclusive use test for a home office require?
notes.back: Using a specific area of the home only for the trade or business.
notes.explanation: The area need not be walled off; a separately identifiable space is enough.
notes.source: Publication 587 (2025), Business Use of Your Home, “Exclusive Use”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: To qualify under the exclusive use test, you must use a specific area of your home only for your trade or business.

notes.front: A self-employed writer works every weekday in a spare bedroom, which also sleeps visiting relatives several times a year. Does the room qualify as a home office?
notes.back: C: no.
notes.choices:
A) Yes: she works there every weekday
B) Yes, for the days without guests
C) No: it fails the exclusive use test
notes.choicesExplained: A meets regular use only. B invents a day-by-day rule.
notes.explanation: Personal use by guests means the area is not used only for business.
notes.source: Publication 587 (2025), Business Use of Your Home, “Exclusive Use”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: To qualify under the exclusive use test, you must use a specific area of your home only for your trade or business.

notes.front: A self-employed electrician does all his wiring at customers’ sites. He uses a home office only and regularly for billing, ordering and bookkeeping, and has no other fixed place for these tasks. Is his home his principal place of business?
notes.back: B: yes.
notes.choices:
A) No: his main work is at customers’ sites
B) Yes
C) No: administrative work never counts
notes.choicesExplained: A and C ignore the rule for administrative or management activities.
notes.explanation: Exclusive, regular administrative use with no other fixed location for it qualifies the home office.
notes.source: Publication 587 (2025), Business Use of Your Home, “Principal Place of Business”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: You use it exclusively and regularly for administrative or management activities of your trade or business. • You have no other fixed location where you conduct substantial administrative or management activities of your trade or business.

notes.front: How is the home office deduction figured under the simplified method?
notes.back: $5 per square foot of qualifying business area, up to 300 square feet.
notes.explanation: It replaces the calculation, allocation and substantiation of actual expenses.
notes.source: Publication 587 (2025), Business Use of Your Home, “Using the Simplified Method”, PDF p. 10
notes.evidence: In most cases, you will figure your deduction by multiplying $5, the prescribed rate, by the area of your home used for a qualified business use. The area you use to figure your deduction is limited to 300 square feet.

notes.front: A consultant uses a 400-square-foot room exclusively and regularly as her principal place of business and chooses the simplified method for 2025. What is her deduction, before any income limit?
notes.choicesExplained: B ignores the 300-square-foot cap. C uses too small an area.
notes.explanation: Area capped at 300 sq ft: 300 × $5 = $1,500.
notes.source: Publication 587 (2025), Business Use of Your Home, “Using the Simplified Method”, PDF p. 10
notes.evidence: The area you use to figure your deduction is limited to 300 square feet.

notes.front: When gross income from the business use of the home is less than total business expenses, what limit applies?
notes.back: Otherwise nondeductible home expenses are limited to that gross income minus other expenses; depreciation is taken last.
notes.explanation: Expenses such as mortgage interest and real estate taxes, deductible anyway, are subtracted first.
notes.source: Publication 587 (2025), Business Use of Your Home, “Deduction Limit”, PDF p. 9
notes.evidence: Your deduction of otherwise nondeductible expenses, such as insurance, utilities, and depreciation of your home (with depreciation of your home taken last) that are allocable to the business, is limited to the gross income from the business use of your home
